scopeNotes: New text needs independent review; earlier hashes do not certify it.
Map endpoints are not historical founding or extinction dates.

The imported destination spans 500 to 600 in southern and eastern Britain. It is a broad cultural map label, not a verified unified state. The wider card covers later developments with dated sections and periods; the imported endpoint does not become an extinction date.

The collective term encompasses changing communities, kingdoms and identities. No genetic result is used to define membership in an ethnicity, to assign political allegiance, or to make a claim about the superiority or purity of any population.

The 2022 Gretzinger paper was read through indexed abstract and substantial full-text passages. Its later correction is acknowledged by the indexed source. The card avoids national replacement percentages, modern-population extrapolations and claims that a cemetery sample represents everyone in Britain.

Hatherdene Close is used as a specific within-cemetery example. Ancestry and birthplace are distinct, and grave goods alone do not diagnose either. The paper’s statistical associations are limited to its samples.

West Stow’s HER gives an approximate 380 to 650 range, while Hoggett’s summary places the settlement from about 420 into the early seventh century and describes a final 600 to 650 phase. The card does not assert a single precise founding or abandonment year. The 450 to 597 period is an approximate interpretive phase within early settlement history.

The HER counts 67 sunken-featured structures and the 2015 article counts 68. No total is repeated without reconciling their coverage. The site is multi-period; Roman kilns and Iron Age remains are not assigned to the Anglo-Saxon phase.

Hoggett’s printed page 46 was rendered and visually inspected, including the SFB 15 photograph and its caption, loom weights on planks and the Hall 1 posthole plan. The card describes preserved remains and supported interpretation, not a certainty about every building’s original superstructure.

The 2015 article is budgeted as one source across architecture, crafts and food. Its suggestion of surplus cloth being traded is marked as interpretation. The plant-impression laboratory report is separately read and its sampling and incorporation warnings retained.

The British Museum’s Sutton Hoo page returned HTTP 403 on opening, but its indexed Silver and gold section and dating caption were available. The card uses only those passages and does not claim to have inspected the complete catalogue or artifacts. The different museum hanging-bowl entry includes inconsistent dating language and was not used to set a precise burial year.

The Sutton Hoo purse group is 37 coins plus three blanks and two ingots, not 42 circulating coins. The bowls’ sixth-century manufacture is separated from the seventh-century burial. Their original routes of transfer and the identity of the buried person are not established by the card.

The British Library catalogue gives circa 700 (695 to 705 metadata), with Eadfrith attribution from a tenth-century colophon and probable Lindisfarne origin. Other proposed sites and chronology remain possible. Aldred’s third-quarter tenth-century gloss is not attributed to the original scribe.

The manuscript’s present nineteenth-century binding is not described as Anglo-Saxon. Its written catalogue was inspected; no independent examination of all folio images, pigments or physical manuscript is claimed.

The map destination is broader than the kingdom conquered in 1066. The ending explicitly names the political ruling order that changed and continued language and community life. No successor link is added without matching historical identity and event-year geometry verification.
Independent historical review, chronology, identity, material interpretation, geometry and depth assessment remain pending.
